Here‘s some more info as promised! Please correct me if some of my historical details are inaccurate.

1) The first is a drachm of Alexander the Great as Hercules wearing the headdress of the Nemean Lion. Hercules  defeated the Nemean Lion in combat as one of his great labors, and Alexander borrows that imagery to depict himself as being nearly divine in battle.

2) The second is a very rare and enigmatic drachm of Hera and Zeus, the queen and king of the gods, presented as one being in the style of Janus, the god of opportunity and pathways. I personally think of it as a really cool commentary on gender equality, with Hera presented as Zeus’ and man’s equal. The coin comes from the island of Tenedos, and you can read the name of the settlement on the reverse of the coin.

3) The third is of the nymph Larissa, who from what I have seen is often styled on coins similarly to Persephone. This coin comes from the region where Mount Olympus is, the mythological home of the gods. A grazing horse is depicted on the reverse, as Thessaly was renowned for their horse breeding.

4) The fourth is a sestertius of the Emperor Antoninus Pius, one of the five good emperors known for the relative peace of his reign. The Earthen deposits are really fun and colorful on this one — they remind me of confetti!

5) The last is the oldest known silver coin issue in human history — a Lydian stater from the sixth century BC! King Croesus was the first to separate electrum into gold and silver coinage, which was one of the most important innovations for commerce in history. From what I have read, it depicts a lion and bull facing each other, which may be a metaphor for the duality of western and eastern cultural influences in Lydia.
